strengths: Clear and timely motivation: the paper highlights a critical deployment issue where reasoning models, which are decode-heavy (|c| + |y| >> |x|), suffer severe performance drops and longer inference times when pruned with standard prompt-based calibration.

Simple, effective, and drop-in methodology: Reasoning-Aware Compression (RAC) naturally aligns the calibration distribution with the on-policy autoregressive generation distribution without needing post-training fine-tuning or distillation.

Comprehensive scaling evaluation across DeepSeek-R1 distilled models ranging from 1.5B to 32B parameters on MATH500 and LiveCodeBench, showing substantial and consistent gains over generic C4 and prompt-only calibration at high sparsity levels (e.g., 40% and 50%).
Insightful diagnostic analysis: Figure 2 effectively visualizes how RAC reduces reconstruction error specifically during the decoding phase on unseen test problems.
Practical throughput and hardware considerations: Appendix Table 4 evaluates 2:4 semi-structured sparsity and FP8 quantization, showing actual inference speedups on Ampere GPUs.
weaknesses: Evaluation is restricted primarily to SparseGPT: while Algorithm 1 suggests applicability to other pruning methods such as Wanda, the empirical validation exclusively uses SparseGPT.

Limited benchmark diversity: the evaluation focuses on MATH500 and LiveCodeBench; including additional challenging math/reasoning benchmarks (such as AIME24, GPQA Diamond, or GSM8K) would strengthen the empirical claims.

Conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental: modifying calibration sets to better reflect test-time activation distributions is an intuitive extension of existing calibration data analyses (e.g., Bandari et al., 2024).

Minor presentation issues: the code repository link in the abstract is missing, and several references in the bibliography are duplicated (e.g., Frantar & Alistarh 2023a/b, Frantar et al. 2022/2023, Zhang et al. 2025a/b).

strengths: Clear, intuitive, and practically relevant motivation: The paper identifies a concrete pathology when compressing long-context reasoning models (such as DeepSeek-R1 distillations), namely that standard pruning causes severe degradation and induces verbose, rambling chains-of-thought.

Sound insight regarding calibration distribution mismatch: Showing that reasoning models are decode-dominated ($|c| + |y| \gg |x|$) and that prompt-only or generic web-text calibration ignores the decode-phase activation distribution is well-reasoned and empirically substantiated.

Comprehensive empirical validation across model scales: The experiments evaluate Qwen-distilled R1 models spanning four sizes (1.5B, 7B, 14B, and 32B) across multiple sparsity levels (20% to 50%) on both mathematical reasoning (MATH-500) and coding (LiveCodeBench).

Informative error diagnostics and practical ablations: The tokenwise error ratio visualization (Figure 2) clearly verifies that RAC mitigates reconstruction error specifically during the decoding phase. Additionally, testing semi-structured 2:4 sparsity with FP8 quantization (Table 4) demonstrates practical throughput benefits on hardware.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is modest: The algorithmic core consists of feeding dense model rollouts (on-policy generation) into the existing SparseGPT calibration pipeline. While effective, using model rollouts to collect calibration data is an intuitive fix rather than a novel compression algorithm.

Narrow compression and model diversity: The empirical evaluation focuses almost exclusively on SparseGPT applied to the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen family. Evaluating other pruning techniques (e.g., Wanda, RIA) or other reasoning model architectures (e.g., LLaMA-based reasoning distillations) would strengthen the generality of the conclusions.

Lack of calibration cost analysis: Collecting on-policy traces of up to 8k tokens per prompt requires substantial dense autoregressive inference prior to pruning. The paper does not report the compute/time overhead required to prepare the RAC calibration set compared to prompt-only or C4 baselines.

Presentation and formatting polish: There are several presentation issues, including an incomplete sentence and URL in the abstract ('Code reproducing the results in the paper can be found at:'), duplicated bibliography entries (e.g., Zhang et al., 2025a/b; Frantar & Alistarh, 2023a/b), and unexplained missing entries in Table 1 (50% sparsity for 32B under C4).

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: The paper identifies a crucial practical paradox in compressing reasoning models—standard post-training pruning leads to degraded accuracy and increased inference latency due to verbose, rambling chains of thought caused by prompt-versus-decode distribution shift.

Simple and effective drop-in methodology: Reasoning-Aware Compression (RAC) requires no fine-tuning or distillation; simply incorporating on-policy generated decode activations into the calibration matrix yields consistent, significant improvements over generic C4 and prompt-only baselines.

Solid empirical evaluation across scales: Experiments cover four model sizes (Qwen-Distill 1.5B, 7B, 14B, and 32B) across multiple sparsity levels (20% to 50%) on both mathematical reasoning (MATH-500) and coding (LiveCodeBench).

Insightful diagnostic and ablation studies: The tokenwise reconstruction error heatmap (Figure 2) clearly validates why RAC succeeds during autoregressive decoding, and the ablations on off-policy traces, 2:4 semi-structured sparsity, and decode limits provide valuable deployment insights.
weaknesses: Narrow algorithm coverage: Although Algorithm 1 mentions applicability to other pruning algorithms such as Wanda, the main evaluation is almost exclusively built around SparseGPT; showing applicability across other post-training pruning (e.g., Wanda, ALPS) and quantization methods (e.g., GPTQ/AWQ) would significantly broaden the paper's impact.

Lack of calibration overhead quantification: Generating on-policy rollouts up to 8,192 tokens during calibration adds computational overhead compared to prompt-only or static C4 calibration. The paper should explicitly report calibration wall-clock times and compute budgets.

Benchmark breadth: Evaluations are restricted to MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench. Evaluating on additional benchmarks (e.g., AIME, GSM8K, or general reasoning tasks like ARC-C) would confirm that the benefits generalize across reasoning types without regressing general language understanding.

Presentation and formatting polish: Incomplete text in the abstract ('Code reproducing the results in the paper can be found at: [blank]'), duplicate reference entries (e.g., Frantar & Alistarh 2023a/b, Zhang et al. 2025a/b), and placing core ablation tables (Tables 3–5) in the appendix while discussing them as main-text sections slightly detract from readability.

strengths: Clear, intuitive, and practically well-motivated core idea: post-training pruning methods traditionally calibrate on input prompt tokens, whereas reasoning models are decode-dominated (|c| + |y| >> |x|), making prompt-only calibration prone to severe distribution shifts.

The proposed Reasoning-Aware Compression (RAC) is simple and drop-in, requiring no changes to underlying pruning algorithms (e.g., SparseGPT, ALPS, WANDA) or expensive retraining/distillation pipelines.
Comprehensive and extensive experimental evaluation across multiple model architectures (DeepSeek-R1 distilled Qwen, DeepSeek-R1 distilled LLaMA, Qwen models), scaling from 1.5B up to 70B parameters.
Evaluations span challenging reasoning tasks (MATH500, AIME-25, LiveCodeBench), multiple pruning algorithms, semi-structured 2:4 sparsity, and FP8 quantization.

Insightful analysis of the runtime pathology where pruned models generate excessively long, rambling chains of thought, and clear demonstration of how RAC combined with token limits alleviates this issue.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is somewhat incremental: modifying calibration data to include self-generated responses (on-policy generation) is an established intuition in imitation learning/distillation and self-calibration, applied here specifically to the calibration set of one-shot pruning.

Calibration overhead is not systematically quantified: generating up to 1M tokens autoregressively with dense models is significantly slower than standard single-forward-pass calibration on fixed text chunks. A breakdown of calibration wall-clock time across model sizes would strengthen the practical evaluation.

Formatting and presentation details need polishing: the abstract contains a dangling placeholder ('Anonymized code can be found at:'), Figure 1 is extremely small and illegible, and some model designations (e.g., 'Qwen3 reasoning models (1.7B, 8B, 14B)') appear non-standard or lack clear citation/specification.

strengths: Clear, timely, and practically important problem formulation: reasoning models exhibit severe performance degradation and counter-intuitive runtime blowups under standard post-training pruning due to repetitive, rambling chain-of-thought (CoT) generation.

Intuitive and plug-and-play solution: Reasoning-Aware Compression (RAC) addresses the inference-time activation distribution shift by incorporating on-policy self-generated CoT tokens into layer-wise calibration, requiring no retraining or distillation.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: the method is thoroughly validated across multiple model families (DeepSeek-R1 Distill Qwen, DeepSeek-R1 LLaMA, and Qwen reasoning models) across diverse scales (1.5B up to 70B), on rigorous reasoning benchmarks (MATH500, AIME-25, LiveCodeBench).

Agnostic across pruning algorithms and formats: RAC consistently improves performance across different pruning algorithms (SparseGPT, WANDA, ALPS) as well as under realistic deployment settings such as 2:4 semi-structured sparsity and FP8 quantization with verified throughput gains.

Insightful diagnostic analysis: Figure 2 provides a compelling token-wise reconstruction error analysis illustrating that RAC effectively suppresses error accumulation during long autoregressive decoding steps.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: augmenting calibration distributions with model rollouts or task completions is a conceptually straightforward fix to activation distribution mismatch, though its specific application and systematic study in reasoning LLM pruning are well-executed.

Evaluation on general-purpose / non-reasoning capabilities is missing: reasoning LLMs are often expected to maintain general knowledge and conversational instruction-following. It is unclear whether calibrating predominantly on math/code CoT traces impairs performance on standard non-reasoning benchmarks (e.g., MMLU, IFEval, or general language perplexity).

Model nomenclature and calibration cost details: the paper refers to 'Qwen3 reasoning models (1.7B, 8B, 14B)', which is unusual given current public releases (e.g., Qwen2.5 or QwQ), requiring clarification. Additionally, reporting concrete wall-clock time for generating the calibration tokens (especially for 32B and 70B models) would better quantify the offline overhead.
Visual presentation in Figure 1: the font sizes on axes and legends in Figure 1 are exceptionally small and hard to read without zooming in significantly.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: As reasoning models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1) generate thousands of decode-time reasoning tokens, studying post-training compression specifically tailored to the decode-heavy distribution is highly relevant.

Interesting empirical insight: The paper documents an important failure mode where aggressive pruning leads to degraded, rambling reasoning paths that actually increase wall-clock inference time due to extended sequence lengths.

Comprehensive empirical scope: The evaluation spans multiple distilled reasoning models (DeepSeek-R1 Qwen and Llama variants), diverse benchmarks (MATH-500, AIME-25, LiveCodeBench), multiple pruning algorithms (SparseGPT, WANDA, ALPS), and includes semi-structured (2:4) sparsity with FP8 quantization.

Detailed analytical ablations: The paper provides informative ablations, such as the token-wise reconstruction error comparison across prompt vs. decode phases (Figure 2), on-policy vs. off-policy trace calibration (Table 7), and decoding token budget caps (Table 8).
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: The proposed RAC method fundamentally consists of running the dense model to generate responses on calibration prompts and appending those hidden states to the calibration activation matrix. Adapting calibration distributions to include generated or downstream task tokens is already a known concept in post-training quantization and pruning.

Questionable model configurations and reproducibility concerns: The paper references a 'Qwen3 reasoning model' family with sizes 1.7B, 8B, and 14B (Tables 2, 4, 9, 10). These do not correspond to any publicly verified open-source release (e.g., Qwen2/2.5 architectures feature 1.5B, 7B, 14B, 32B, 72B), creating significant confusion and raising concerns regarding reproducibility. Furthermore, the repository link in the abstract is left blank ('Anonymized code can be found at:').

Conflation of kernel speedup and sequence length in runtime reporting: Most tables report wall-clock runtime for unstructured sparsity, where the acceleration/slowdown is almost entirely an artifact of how many tokens the model outputs before hitting EOS or maximum budget, rather than actual inference acceleration. While Table 6 examines 2:4 structured sparsity, hardware speedups and latency benchmarks under standard serving frameworks (e.g., vLLM or TensorRT-LLM) remain underexplored.

Overhead of calibration phase: Collecting up to 8,192 on-policy tokens per prompt across 1M calibration tokens requires substantial dense autoregressive inference passes. The paper should quantify the compute and time overhead of RAC calibration compared to standard prompt-only calibration.

Bibliographic anomalies: Citations contain questionable dates and formatting (e.g., citing Zhang et al. with arXiv ID '2504.02010', indicating April 2025, which appears anomalous depending on submission timing).
